falsesharing:sc:2013: Reception splits along the paper's two identities. The false-sharing detectors that followed — PREDATOR, Cheetah, LASER, Featherlight — cite it chiefly to differentiate their own approaches, contrasting precise memory-level analysis with its performance-event classification. The machine-learning identity found a more direct successor: the zero-positive learning line, from diagnosing software performance regressions through AutoPerf and AutoCon, treats it as the baseline for learned detection of performance anomalies, and DR-BW lists it among precedents for supervised learning over hardware counters. Beyond these two threads the citations are brief mentions, and the record as a whole is modest and concentrated in the performance-tools community.
amarasinghe:micro:1996: Citers treat the article less as an argument than as a handle for the SUIF parallelizer: most substantive citations come from work that uses the system. SUIF Explorer and compiler-directed page coloring build on the infrastructure within the Stanford orbit, a long line of embedded-systems and energy-optimization studies by Kandemir and colleagues cites the article for the compiler their experiments run on, and hardware/software co-compilation efforts from FPGA module mapping to the Nymble system do the same. The article's own thesis — that architects should design for parallelizing compilers — draws less direct engagement, surviving mainly in occasional passing references.
bruening:cgo:2005: External reception likewise comes from builders. The dynamic binary translation community treats the paper as a reference on code-cache consistency and capacity: the DynamoRIO line extended it to thread-shared and process-shared, persistent code caches, while independent systems engage it on its own ground — fragment-cache management for embedded scratchpads and work on reducing pressure in bounded DBT code caches position their schemes against it, and HDTrans, generators of low-overhead binary translators, and process-level redundancy work on transient fault tolerance cite its measurements as evidence. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the same literature; almost nothing cites the paper from outside the community that manages code caches. The DynamoRIO system lives on in the DynamoRIO/dynamorio repository.
barua:toc:2001: The citing record is modest and settles mainly in embedded-systems compilation, where software-managed memory outlived Raw. Barua's subsequent work on scratch-pad memory allocation engages the bank-disambiguation techniques in detail, Cho, Paek, and Whalley position their memory-bank assignment methods for digital signal processors against it, and a survey of compiling for reconfigurable computing places it among approaches to software-exposed memory. The rest of the citations are passing mentions, several from the pointer-analysis literature. Few works extend the techniques themselves; the article is cited for what it showed — that a compiler can place data well when memory banks are visible to software.
mendis:pldi:2015: Later work cites Helium mainly as a fixed point in the design space of lifting: papers on raising legacy code to higher-level forms — verified lifting of stencil computations, automatic translation of image-processing libraries to Halide, trace-based affine reconstruction of codes — differentiate themselves from its dynamic, trace-driven approach, and Collie and O'Boyle's gray-box program lifting measures against it. As many citations name it as proof that stripped, optimized binaries can be lifted at all, motivating work from matching legacy code to heterogeneous APIs to hardware FFT accelerators. Direct reuse is rare — a temporal-blocking stencil study builds on it — so the paper stands as a demonstrated endpoint rather than a platform.
moritz:ims:2000: The framework's most direct descendants are Cool-Mem and Cool-Cache, which carry compiler-managed caching into energy-efficient embedded and multimedia processors. In the wider literature FlexCache figures as the software-managed pole of the scratch-pad memory debate: work on static and dynamic scratch-pad allocation positions its schemes against the framework's virtualized caching, one such allocator takes it as a baseline, and the textbook Memory Systems: Cache, DRAM, Disk records it in surveying alternatives to hardware caches. The remaining citations are brief mentions in the compiler-managed memory literature — a small record, but one anchored in the community that debated how software should manage on-chip memory.
kiriansky:pact:2016: Reception lies less in other compilers than in computer architecture. Hardware proposals for irregular memory access cite milk as the software point of comparison: PHI differentiates its approach from milk's, täkō measures against it as a baseline, DX100 reuses its workloads, and a survey of sparse-matrix accelerators picks up the idea. Peripheral mentions cluster in the same territory — locality-enhancing systems from hardware-accelerated graph-traversal scheduling to SpMV vectorization list DRAM-conscious clustering among software answers to the random-access problem. The record is small but placed where the technique aimed: papers about making indirect references cheap.
lerer:dev:2010: The answer — not without training — is what the citing literature carries forward. Voice-interface work in ICTD and HCI cites the study chiefly as evidence about what untrained users can operate: 99DOTS and Learn2Earn draw on its findings, a review of mobile-phone data collection in developing countries examines its design lessons, and voice-forum and voice-based literacy systems such as Sangeet Swara mention it when surveying IVR precedents. Gurgaon Idol engages it in more detail, situating its findings within the design of a voice-based community platform. The engagement is mostly brief, a supporting citation in related-work sections, but consistent: the paper serves as the cautionary datum on touchtone interfaces for first-time users.
thies:www:2002: TEK's citations are few and come chiefly from the community that took up the problem of web access under poor connectivity. RuralCafe, studies of web search and browsing behavior under poor connectivity, and the analysis of WWW traffic in Cambodia and Ghana position their designs and findings against its email-based approach, while the Delay-Tolerant Networking Architecture and work on optimizing high-latency links mention it in passing among asynchronous-access precedents. The engagement is mostly brief, but it places the system among the early reference points for intermittent and low-bandwidth web delivery.
tyler:ppopp:2016: Subsequent citing work keeps it in that role of reference point. Stencil papers measure against it — a roofline-guided multi-stencil CFD solver and instruction-stream scheduling work for stencils on ARM processors take it as the distributed baseline — while distributed machine-learning systems, among them work on dataflow-graph partitioning for very large models and on breaking the computation-communication abstraction barrier, position their handling of communication relative to its schedule-level approach. One effort built on the system itself, extending it to distributed and heterogeneous SAR backprojection with Halide. The record is small but a good share of it is substantive: the paper serves as the point of comparison for expressing distribution in the schedule.
soule:debs:2013: Reception of the relaxation is modest and comes mostly by way of example. Stream-language work cites the paper when cataloguing how systems handle dynamic rates: the SPL language description and the River intermediate language discuss its hybrid scheduling, LaminarIR positions its compile-time queues against it, and work on mapping streaming applications to multi-CPU and GPU processors lists it among scheduling approaches. Few works build on the scheduler itself; in the citing literature the paper stands as one documented answer to the question of combining static optimization with dynamic rates.
ariya:cc:2002: Externally, the deepest engagement builds with the compiler itself. A line of secure-computation systems — Shechi, Decor, and a secure multiple-imputation pipeline — implements on top of Codon, and Vectron uses it as the substrate for auto-vectorizing dynamic programming; interpreter-testing work and an empirical study of the performance and energy of compiled Python treat it as a system under test. The rest of the record is thinner: Python-compilation papers such as HiPy reuse its benchmarks or compare against it, and list mentions place it among approaches to accelerating Python. The citation record is small, but its substantive uses are genuine system-building, and the compiler lives on in exaloop/codon.
anderson:ppopp:1995: The judged portion of the citation record concentrates in the locality-optimization literature: the sustained line of work by Kandemir, Ramanujam, and Choudhary on integrating loop and data transformations defines its frameworks against this paper's, returning to it in a compiler algorithm for optimizing locality in loop nests, matrix-based approaches to global locality, and an interprocedural framework. Work on tuning compiler optimizations for simultaneous multithreading positions itself the same way, and the remaining citations are brief mentions in later data-layout work. Most of the external record has not been judged, so the picture is partial; what it shows is a paper that combined loop-and-data frameworks named as their point of departure.
zhao:cgo:2008: What the citing literature took up is PiPA's central idea — decoupling analysis from execution and running it as a parallel pipeline — more than the prototype itself. TaintPipe carries pipelined processing into symbolic taint analysis, ShadowReplica positions its own decoupled taint tracking relative to PiPA, and work on dynamic binary parallelization and on data-flow tracking systems adopts the compact-profile approach. A concurrent dynamic analysis framework for multicore hardware measures itself against PiPA directly. The remaining citations are mostly brief, placing the system in lists of attempts to hide instrumentation cost with spare cores.
chen:asplos:2021: Among citing works VeGen figures chiefly as a marker in the vectorization literature: papers on tensor compilers and SIMD code generation list it among approaches that reach beyond packed SIMD, usually in a sentence or two. The substantive engagement comes from synthesis-based vectorizers and instruction-selection work — Coyote, vector instruction selection for digital signal processors using program synthesis, Minotaur, and Hydride — which position their techniques against VeGen's generation of a vectorizer from instruction semantics. The record is modest and skews toward brief mentions, but the works that do engage are those pursuing the same question of retargetable vector code generation. The implementation is available as ychen306/vegen, and the paper carries Artifacts Evaluated & Functional and Results Reproduced badges.
drake:ipdps:2006: Elsewhere the decoder's afterlife is chiefly as a workload. The StreamIt MPEG-2 implementation joined the benchmark suites of compiler and architecture studies — a comparative evaluation of memory models for chip multiprocessors and Sigma*'s symbolic learning of stream filters both run it — and stream-language papers such as Canals cite the paper when arguing that video codecs suit the streaming model. Beyond these uses the citations are mostly list entries in discussions of stream-programming applications. The record is modest, but the program outlived its publication as a shared test case, which is what an application paper aims for. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure, including this decoder, is preserved in the bthies/streamit repository.
rawn:oopsla:2021: Beyond the group's own citing papers, external engagement is limited in volume but concentrated at the core: the paper's closest readers are builders. SpDISTAL carries the approach into distributed sparse tensor computation, the compilation of shape operators on sparse arrays extends the theory itself, FuseFlow applies it to sparse deep learning on streaming dataflow, and compilers for fused relational operations on multisets and for tensor-algebra representation of RTL simulation adopt its generalized sparse iteration. Around that core, SparseTIR and the MLIR sparse tensor work discuss it in detail, a polyhedral compiler for sparse tensor contraction measures against it, and the remaining citations are brief mentions in the sparse-compilation literature. The implementation lives on the array_algebra branch of the taco repository.
jaeyeon:asplos:2023: That framing — format and schedule tuned as one — is what the citing literature takes from the paper. Subsequent sparse-tensor autotuners measure themselves against WACO: AutoSparse, RASSM, UniSparTa, and SparseZETA use it as a baseline, STile differentiates its hybrid-format search from it, and COGNATE extends the approach with transfer learning toward emerging hardware. Outside that circle the citations are brief, listing WACO among learned approaches to sparse computation. The record is small but pointed: most of its substantive citations come from systems competing on exactly the problem the paper posed. The implementation is available at nullplay/Workload-Aware-Co-Optimization, and an evaluated artifact accompanies the paper on Zenodo.
stephenson:eurogp:2003: With the PLDI paper absorbing the primary citations, the EuroGP version's own record is small and lives where it was addressed: the evolutionary-computation literature cites it as the compiler example. Harman and colleagues' survey of search-based software engineering, Burke and colleagues' treatment of hyper-heuristics, and a survey of compiler autotuning using machine learning all place it among applications of genetic programming, while papers on genetic instruction scheduling and on optimization-space exploration position their approaches near it. Few citations engage the evolved priority functions themselves; the paper is received as an instance of an idea rather than as an artifact.
goslp: External reception is modest and concentrated where one would expect, in the SLP vectorization literature. The line of SLP refinements from Porpodas and colleagues — VW-SLP and Super-Node SLP — positions its heuristics against goSLP's global ILP formulation, and Coyote does the same for vectorizing encrypted arithmetic circuits. Elsewhere the paper appears in lists of auto-vectorization work or as evidence about the state of SLP vectorizers; an evaluation of compilers' capability of automatic vectorization gives it a closer reading. The citations are few, but the substantive ones come from the community refining SLP itself. An evaluated and functional artifact accompanies the paper.
ahrens_autoscheduling_2022: The citation record is short and mostly glancing: sparse-compilation systems such as SparseTIR, the Sparse Abstract Machine, and Mosaic cite it in passing among schedulers and cost models for sparse code. The engaged citations, though, are the audience the paper addresses. SparseAuto adopts its ideas for auto-scheduling with recursive loop-nest restructuring, Galley builds on it for query optimization over sparse tensor programs, a fast autoscheduler for sparse machine-learning frameworks measures against it, and the indexed-streams formalization of fused contraction programs cites its results. With Looplets taking the protocolized notation as its input language, the paper sits at the base of a small line of asymptotic-cost scheduling work. The implementation is preserved as Pigeon.jl, and a reusable artifact accompanies the paper on Zenodo.
amarasinghe:siam:1995: Most of the works citing this overview have not been judged, so its reception can be read only in part. In the judged record the paper serves two roles: as a pointer to SUIF as working infrastructure — cited by work on speculative parallelism for multiprocessors and by the OlyMPIx parallelization tool as the compiler they start from — and as an entry in surveys of the field, from the ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems account of data and memory optimization for embedded systems to reviews of parallelization tools. Both roles attach to the SUIF project as a whole rather than to this paper's particular argument.
bhive: The suite found the use it was built for: the citing literature consists largely of work that runs on BHive rather than work that merely mentions it. Abel and Reineke validate their throughput predictors and the uiCA simulator on it, DiffTune tunes CPU-simulator parameters against its measurements, COMET uses it to explain neural cost models, and several studies of transformer models over low-level programs draw their basic blocks from it; a microbenchmarking toolkit adopts its measurement methodology. The community is small and concentrated in basic-block performance modeling, but within that community BHive serves as common ground for validation. The suite and its profiler are available at ithemal/bhive.
chan:sc:2009: The external record is small and mostly illustrative. Surveys of machine learning in compiler optimization and of automated multigrid-solver development cite the work as an example of autotuning over algorithmic choice with accuracy as a tunable parameter, and floating-point precision-tuning work credits the same idea. Within multigrid itself, papers on optimizing geometric multigrid for multicore and manycore processors and on communication-avoiding operators position their approaches against it rather than build on it. Direct extension of the method came from within the project, so the external reception is citation-as-example rather than adoption — a paper known for its idea more than its artifact. The implementation lives on in the petabricks/petabricks repository.
ansel:xrds:2010: The piece draws light citation of its own — the research credit flows to the PLDI paper — and its reception is correspondingly modest. Where it is cited, it serves as an accessible reference for PetaBricks and for autotuning in general: SPIRAL's account of extreme performance portability lists it among autotuning systems, papers on autotuning divide-and-conquer stencils and on autotuning exascale applications do the same, and work on programming and mapping strategies for runtime-adaptable embedded computing gives it a closer reading. The pattern suits the genre — an introduction written for students, cited when authors want an approachable entry to the idea. The PetaBricks implementation is available at petabricks/petabricks on GitHub.
